sections.overview: Archips xylosteana is a leaf-rolling moth in the tortricid family, Tortricidae. In English it is called the Variegated Golden Tortrix.
sections.identification: British accounts give a wingspan of 15–21 mm for males and 16–24 mm for females; a general field guide gives 15–23 mm overall. Males usually show stronger contrast in the brown-ochre forewing pattern, while females are often more subdued. It resembles Archips crataegana, but is usually smaller and more variegated, whereas that relative is broader-winged and browner. The caterpillar is grey-white to bluish with a greenish cast and a dark head; a French forest-health note reports that it develops from April in a leaf rolled across the midrib. A German forestry account gives larval length as about 15–20 mm. Caterpillars can be confused with Archips podana and Archips rosana, whose larvae use similar food plants and are difficult to tell apart by appearance alone.
sections.habitat: It occurs in woodland and gardens across much of Britain. German accounts also record it along woodland edges and in hedgerows and other tree-rich gardens.
sections.diet: The caterpillars are polyphagous on deciduous trees and shrubs, including oak, elm, lime, hazel, maple, ash and fruit trees. They feed inside a rolled or spun leaf, which gives the larva shelter as it eats.
sections.behavior: Adults fly from just before dusk into the night and are mainly seen in July and August in Britain. German accounts place the adult flight more broadly from June to August, showing that dates vary across the range.
sections.reproduction: A British species account reports that the eggs overwinter. A French forest-health note says the young caterpillars develop from April inside a leaf rolled across the midrib.
sections.ecology: In some years and suitable forest settings, larval numbers can rise sharply and cause heavy leaf loss, especially on oaks; this is an episodic outbreak, not the normal condition everywhere.
sections.conservation: A British regional account describes the species as common in woodland and gardens across the British Isles; that frequency label is regional and does not establish a global trend.
